opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core idea is that we usually look at a neural network only through its inputs and outputs: we feed in data, check accuracy, and move on. But the weights themselves are a very rich data modality. Every trained model is a point in a high-dimensional space, and when you train many models, a whole population of them, you start to see structure. Models don't land randomly; they form trajectories and clusters, and those patterns carry information about how the model was trained and how well it will behave.

So in our group we started building what we call model zoos. These are large, systematically generated collections of trained networks where we vary things like initialization, hyperparameters, and datasets, and we save checkpoints along the training trajectory. Once you have that, you can treat the weights as a dataset and learn on top of it. We've trained representation learning models, hyper-representations, that take the weights of a network as input and learn an embedding of the model itself.

What's exciting is what you can do with that embedding. You can predict properties of a model, like its test accuracy, its generalization gap, or which hyperparameters were used, just by looking at the weights, without running any data through it. That's useful for model analysis, for auditing, and for spotting models that are going to underperform early in training.

Then there's the generative side. If you've learned the distribution of good weights, you can sample new weights from it. We've shown that you can generate initializations that train faster or reach better performance than standard random initialization, or produce ensembles of diverse, well-performing models cheaply. So instead of always starting from scratch, you start from a region of weight space you already know is promising.

One of the hard parts, and where the geometry really matters, is symmetry. Neural networks have a lot of it: you can permute neurons in a layer and get exactly the same function with completely different weights. If you ignore that, your weight-space model gets confused, because functionally identical networks look far apart. So we've had to build augmentations and architectures that respect or exploit those symmetries, and that turned out to be key to making these representations work.

Longer term, I see this as a step toward learning from the experience of training itself. We train millions of models as a community and mostly throw that knowledge away. If we can understand the geometry of weight space well enough, we can reuse it to make training more efficient, more predictable, and maybe a bit less of a dark art.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here. So the way I think about it is this: when we train a neural network, what we're really doing is moving a point around in a very high-dimensional space, the space of all possible weight configurations. Every training run traces a path through that space, and where you end up depends on your initialization, your optimizer, your data, your hyperparameters. For a long time the field treated the final weights as a kind of black box artifact, something you just use for inference and otherwise don't look at. What we've been doing in my group is treating those weights themselves as data, and asking what structure that space actually has.

And it turns out there's a lot of structure. If you train hundreds or thousands of small models, what we call model zoos, with different seeds and different hyperparameters, and then you look at the weights, you find that models cluster. Models trained with similar learning rates or similar optimizers end up in similar regions, and you can actually predict properties of a model, like its test accuracy, how far along in training it is, or whether it's going to generalize well, just from the weights, without ever running the model on data. That tells you the geometry is encoding something meaningful about the training process.

Why does that help us improve training? A few ways. First, diagnostically. If you can read off from the weights that a model is heading toward a bad basin, or is overfitting, you can intervene early rather than waiting on a validation curve. Second, there's this symmetry structure that's very important to understand. Neural networks have permutation symmetries, you can swap neurons in a layer and get a functionally identical network, and scaling symmetries in things like ReLU networks. So many different points in weight space are actually the same function. Once you factor those out, the landscape looks much simpler, and things like mode connectivity, where two independently trained models can be connected by a low-loss path, start to make much more sense. That has practical consequences for model merging, for averaging weights, for ensembling without paying the full inference cost.

And third, the direction I'm most excited about, is generative. If you learn a representation of weight space, say with a hyper-representation or a diffusion model over weights, you can sample new models. You can generate initializations that are already in a good region, so training is faster, or generate weights for a new task by conditioning on a small amount of information. Essentially you're learning a prior over good solutions, which is something gradient descent from random init just doesn't have.

So to summarize, I'd say weight-space geometry turns training from something we observe from the outside, via loss curves, into something we can inspect and manipulate directly. We're still early, the dimensionality is brutal and scaling this to very large models is an open challenge, but I think it's one of the more under-explored angles for understanding why deep learning works at all.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is that we usually understand a neural network through its behavior: we give it an input and look at the output. But the weights themselves are the result of learning. So studying their geometry gives us another way to ask what happened during training and how two training runs differ.

There is a complication, though: two networks can implement the same function and still look very different in weight space. You can permute hidden units, for example, without changing the computation. So a simple distance between two sets of weights can be misleading. We need to understand those symmetries before we can interpret the geometry.

Once we do that, we can investigate whether different solutions are connected through regions of low loss, which directions are sensitive to changes, and how optimization moves through that space. That can help us reason about stability and potentially guide how we initialize, combine, or update models.

For me, the opportunity is to turn that understanding into better training decisions. But the geometry has to be connected back to actual behavior—especially generalization. A geometric property is useful when it tells us something reliable about how the network performs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting shift is to look at the neural network itself as a data point. Usually, we study the data going into a network and the predictions coming out. But training produces this very high-dimensional collection of weights, and we can ask: What structure is there? How does that structure relate to the behavior of the model?

One challenge is that different weights can represent exactly the same function. If you permute neurons and adjust the connections accordingly, the network’s behavior doesn’t change. So simply measuring the distance between two sets of weights can be misleading. We need to understand those symmetries before we can interpret the geometry.

If we get that right, we can start studying training trajectories, comparing solutions across runs, and asking which properties are associated with generalization or robustness. And then the practical question becomes: Can that understanding help us choose a better initialization, transfer knowledge between models, or guide optimization toward useful solutions more efficiently?

For me, that’s the opportunity: moving from observing what training does to finding structure that we can actually use to improve it.
